runs.acceptance: Targeted cost reduction observed; promoted to candidate14 for unchanged full release gate.
runs.nativeIntervalLimit: The last partial zoom action became slower; no uniform end-to-end speedup claim.

conclusions: The confirmed native direction controls and exact zoom queue are retained. The initial matched-baseline, backing-density and RTT-size diagnostics all failed the unchanged settling gate.
Software backing-density reduction has no demonstrated improvement; the failed run never recorded its post-activation buffer dimensions.
Smaller terrain source tileSize changes RTT granularity and DEM LOD; this diagnostic still failed and is not accepted for production.
Single runs on separate runners do not establish statistical speed differences.
The software pitch 30 policy was applied but did not pass the same high-zoom transition; it was not accepted for production.
The unchanged application reached zoom 18 in the process CPU diagnostic. This cold diagnostic success does not replace the full five-profile release gate.

Untraced high zoom actions consumed 34.98, 45.49 and 26.93 cumulative CPU seconds in the GPU process, averaging 3.52, 3.50 and 3.67 logical cores respectively. Renderer CPU was under one second on those same untraced intervals. This demonstrates expensive software GPU-process work, not its precise draw/texture cause.
All observed CPU intervals retained a visible focused document; actual numeric pitch was not instrumented in this CPU baseline.

The vector slicing candidate was rejected: untraced 14.905→15.905 and 16.905→17.905 actions consumed more GPU-process CPU and took longer than the corresponding CPU baseline; the latter timed out. None of the earlier density, terrain-source-size, pitch or slicing variants is merged into the release.

Public GPU queries identify 2048-square offscreen hillshade rasterization as the dominant sampled operation: eight calls cost 2102.931 ms, compared with 111.042 ms for eight terrain mesh draws. These bounded samples are not a total-cost estimate.

The current installed SDK compiles one hillshade illumination source despite three configured direction and altitude values; a claimed three-to-one light optimization was rejected before implementation.

The distinct SwiftShader-only RTT quality factor candidate was measured at actual1024-square targets while preserving screen/depth resolution, DEM, terrain coverage and mesh. Eight hillshade samples cost43.1% less and eight mipmap samples67.1% less, including lower medians. Terrain drape samples and the final partial zoom action were slower; these bounded observations do not establish uniform speed or full release acceptance. Candidate14 subsequently passed the unchanged full native gate and was published; see the separate exact-source final receipt.
